# Chapter 6: Contiguity

Contiguity is **asymptotic absolute continuity**. It allows us to obtain the limiting distribution of statistics under a sequence of laws $Q_n$ from their limiting behavior under another sequence of laws $P_n$. Typically, $P_n$ represents the null hypothesis and $Q_n$ represents a sequence of alternatives.

## 6.1 Likelihood Ratios

::: {.callout-note title="Definition"}
### Absolute continuity

A probability measure $Q$ is absolutely continuous with respect to $P$ if every event that is impossible under $P$ is also impossible under $Q$:

$$
P(A)=0\implies Q(A)=0.
$$

Notation: $Q\ll P$.

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Definition"}
### Orthogonality

The measures $P$ and $Q$ are orthogonal if they live on disjoint parts of the sample space.

Notation:

$$
P\perp Q.
$$

There exist disjoint sets $\Omega_P$ and $\Omega_Q$ such that

$$
P(\Omega_Q)=0,\qquad Q(\Omega_P)=0.
$$

:::

### Supports of the measures

Suppose $P$ and $Q$ have densities $p$ and $q$ with respect to a common measure $\mu$. Define

$$
\Omega_P={p>0},\qquad \Omega_Q={q>0}.
$$

The overlap

$$
\Omega_P\cap\Omega_Q
$$

is the part of the sample space on which both measures place mass.

The region

$$
{p=0,\ q>0}
$$

contains outcomes that are possible under $Q$ but impossible under $P$.

::: {.callout-note title="Definition"}
<span id="eq-lebesgue-decomposition"></span>

6.1 $Q^a(A) = Q\left(A \cap \{ p > 0\} \right); \qquad Q^\perp (A) = Q\left( A \cap \{p = 0\}\right)$

:::

::: {.callout-important title="Lemma"}
### 6.2 Lemma: Lebesgue decomposition

- Suppose $P$ and $Q$ are probability measures with densities $p$ and $q$ with respect to a common measure $\mu$.
- The measure $Q$ can be decomposed into an absolutely continuous part and an orthogonal part, defined in [(6.1)](#eq-lebesgue-decomposition):
1. $Q=Q^a+Q^\perp, \qquad Q^a\ll P,\qquad Q^\perp\perp P.$
2. The absolutely continuous part: $Q^a(A)=\int_A\frac{q}{p}\,dP$ for every measurable set $A$
3. $Q^a\ll P$ iff $Q(p = 0) = 0$ if and only if $\int (q/p) dP = 1$

These parts are defined by:

$$
Q^a(A)=Q(A\cap{p>0}),\qquad Q^\perp(A)=Q(A\cap{p=0}).
$$

:::

In general,

$$
E_P\frac{dQ}{dP}\leq 1.
$$

Equality holds exactly when

$$
Q\ll P.
$$

For a nonnegative measurable function $f$,

$$
\int f,dQ\geq\int f\frac{dQ}{dP},dP.
$$

The inequality may be strict because the right-hand side cannot recover the part of $Q$ supported on ${p=0}$.

## 6.2 Contiguity

If $Q\ll P,$ then the distribution of a random vector $X$ under $Q$ can be recovered from its joint distribution with the likelihood ratio under $P$:

$$
E_Qf(X)=E_P\left[f(X)\frac{dQ}{dP}\right].
$$

Equivalently,

$$
Q(X\in B)=E_P\left[1_B(X)\frac{dQ}{dP}\right].
$$

- The likelihood ratio therefore acts as a weight that transforms the $P$-distribution into the $Q$-distribution.

::: {.callout-note title="Result"}
### Definition 6.3

The sequence $Q_n$ is contiguous with respect to $P_n$ if

$$
P_n(A_n)\to 0\implies Q_n(A_n)\to 0
$$

for every sequence of measurable events $A_n$.

Notation: $Q_n\triangleleft P_n.$

- Thus, no sequence of events can become asymptotically impossible under $P_n$ while retaining nonvanishing probability under $Q_n$.
- The sequences are mutually contiguous if

$$
Q_n\triangleleft P_n\qquad\text{and}\qquad P_n\triangleleft Q_n.
$$

Notation: $P_n\triangleleft\triangleright Q_n.$

:::

- Absolute continuity concerns a single pair of measures:

$$
P(A)=0\implies Q(A)=0.
$$

- Contiguity concerns sequences of measures:

$$
P_n(A_n)\to 0\implies Q_n(A_n)\to 0.
$$

- Contiguous sequences need not be close in total variation. Contiguity only requires that asymptotically negligible events under one sequence are also negligible under the other.

---

::: {.callout-important title="Lemma"}
### Lemma 6.4: Le Cam’s First Lemma {#lemma-le-cam-first}

The following statements are equivalent.

1. Contiguity $Q_n\triangleleft P_n.$
2. The inverse likelihood ratio does not converge toward zero:

    If, along a subsequence $\frac{dP_n}{dQ_n}\overset{Q_n}{\rightsquigarrow}U,$ then $P(U>0)=1.$ Thus, the limiting inverse likelihood ratio cannot place mass at zero.

3. The likelihood ratio has limiting mean one:
If, along a subsequence, $\frac{dQ_n}{dP_n}\overset{P_n}{\rightsquigarrow}V,$ then $\text{E} V = 1$.
Because likelihood ratios are nonnegative and satisfy $E_{P_n}\frac{dQ_n}{dP_n}\leq 1,$ a limiting mean below one would represent probability mass under $Q_n$ that disappears from the perspective of $P_n$.
4. Convergence in probability transfers: For every sequence of statistics $T_n$, $T_n\overset{P_n}{\to}0\implies T_n\overset{Q_n}{\to}0.$
More generally, conclusions stated in terms of events whose probabilities converge to zero under $P_n$ continue to hold under $Q_n$.

- Le Cam’s first lemma is primarily used to establish contiguity by studying likelihood-ratio limits.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Example"}
### Example 6.5: Asymptotic Log Normality {#example-asymptotic-log-normality}

- Suppose that, under $Q_n$, $\frac{dP_n}{dQ_n}\overset{Q_n}{\rightsquigarrow}e^{N(\mu,\sigma^2)}.$
- Because a lognormal random variable is strictly positive, $Q_n\triangleleft P_n.$
- The sequences are mutually contiguous if and only if $\mu=-\frac{1}{2}\sigma^2.$
- This follows because $Ee^{N(\mu,\sigma^2)}=e^{\mu+\frac{1}{2}\sigma^2},$ which equals one exactly when $\mu=-\frac{1}{2}\sigma^2.$
- The appearance of a normal log likelihood ratio with mean equal to minus one-half its variance is central in smooth parametric models.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Theorem"}
### Theorem 6.6: Abstract Change of Measure {#theorem-change-of-measure}

- Suppose $Q_n\triangleleft P_n$ and, under $P_n$, $\left(X_n,\frac{dQ_n}{dP_n}\right)\overset{P_n}{\rightsquigarrow}(X,V).$
- Define a measure $L$ by $L(B)=E[1_B(X)V].$
- Then $L$ is a probability measure and, under $Q_n$, $X_n\overset{Q_n}{\rightsquigarrow}L.$
- Under $P_n$, the limiting likelihood ratio $V$ reweights the limiting distribution of $X$.
- For suitable functions $f$, $\int f,dL=E[f(X)V].$

Thus:

1. Find the joint limit of the statistic and likelihood ratio under $P_n$.
2. Weight the limiting $P_n$distribution by $V$.
3. The weighted distribution is the limiting distribution under $Q_n$.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Lemma"}
### Example 6.7: Le Cam’s Third Lemma {#lemma-le-cam-third}

- Suppose that, under $P_n$, $\left(X_n,\log\frac{dQ_n}{dP_n}\right)\overset{P_n}{\rightsquigarrow}N_{k+1}\left(\begin{pmatrix}\mu \\ -\frac{1}{2}\sigma^2\end{pmatrix},\begin{pmatrix}\Sigma&\tau\\ \tau^T&\sigma^2\end{pmatrix}\right).$
- Then, under $Q_n$, $X_n\overset{Q_n}{\rightsquigarrow}N_k(\mu+\tau,\Sigma).$

Under the alternative:

- The asymptotic covariance matrix remains $\Sigma.$
- The asymptotic mean changes from $\mu$ to $\mu+\tau.$
- Here, $\tau=\operatorname{Cov}\left(X,\log\frac{dQ_n}{dP_n}\right)$ in the limiting joint normal distribution.
- Thus, moving from $P_n$ to $Q_n$ shifts the limiting mean by the asymptotic covariance between the statistic and the log likelihood ratio.
    - By the [continuous mapping theorem](chapter-2.qmd#theorem-continuous-mapping), $\left(X_n,\frac{dQ_n}{dP_n}\right)\overset{P_n}{\rightsquigarrow}(X,e^W),$ where $W\sim N\left(-\frac{1}{2}\sigma^2,\sigma^2\right).$
    - Because $\text{E}e^W=1,$ Le Cam’s first lemma gives mutual contiguity, and [Theorem 6.6](#theorem-change-of-measure) gives the tilted limiting distribution.
:::
